39|BACKGROUND
40|Androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) has been the backbone of treatment for
41|metastatic prostate cancer since the 1940s. We assessed whether concomitant
42|treatment with ADT plus docetaxel would result in longer overall survival than that
43|with ADT alone.
44|METHODS
45|We assigned men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer to receive
46|either ADT plus docetaxel (at a dose of 75 mg per square meter of body-surface
47|area every 3 weeks for six cycles) or ADT alone. The primary objective was to test
48|the hypothesis that the median overall survival would be 33.3% longer among
49|patients receiving docetaxel added to ADT early during therapy than among pa-
50|tients receiving ADT alone.
51|RESULTS
52|A total of 790 patients (median age, 63 years) underwent randomization. After a
53|median follow-up of 28.9 months, the median overall survival was 13.6 months
54|longer with ADT plus docetaxel (combination therapy) than with ADT alone (57.6
55|months vs. 44.0 months; hazard ratio for death in the combination group, 0.61;
56|95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47 to 0.80; P<0.001). The median time to bio-
57|chemical, symptomatic, or radiographic progression was 20.2 months in the com-
58|bination group, as compared with 11.7 months in the ADT-alone group (hazard
59|ratio, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.72; P<0.001). The rate of a prostate-specific antigen
60|level of less than 0.2 ng per milliliter at 12 months was 27.7% in the combination
61|group versus 16.8% in the ADT-alone group (P<0.001). In the combination group,
62|the rate of grade 3 or 4 febrile neutropenia was 6.2%, the rate of grade 3 or 4
63|infection with neutropenia was 2.3%, and the rate of grade 3 sensory neuropathy
64|and of grade 3 motor neuropathy was 0.5%.
65|CONCLUSIONS
66|Six cycles of docetaxel at the beginning of ADT for metastatic prostate cancer re-
67|sulted in significantly longer overall survival than that with ADT alone. (Funded by
68|the National Cancer Institute and others; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00309985.)

5|egressions of metastatic prostate
6|cancer were first documented in the 1940s
7|and were achieved with surgical castra-
8|tion; subsequently, androgen-deprivation therapy
9|(ADT) became the mainstay of therapy.1 Attempts
10|to improve the efficacy or decrease the treatment
11|burden of ADT have included the use of anti
12|androgens alone, intermittent dosing of ADT,
13|and the use of an antiandrogen combined with
14|medical or surgical castration.2-4 A meta-analysis
15|revealed an increase in survival of 3 percentage
16|points at 5 years with concurrent use of a non-
17|steroidal antiandrogen at the time of initiation
18|of ADT.2 However, resistance to ADT occurs in
19|most patients, with the result that the median
20|survival among patients with metastatic prostate
21|cancer is approximately 3 years.5,6 In patients
22|with resistance to ADT, docetaxel therapy re-
23|sulted in a median survival that was approxi-
24|mately 2.5 months longer than that with mito-
25|xantrone and prednisone.7,8
26|Prior studies of chemotherapy plus ADT, which
27|did not show a benefit, were small studies that
28|involved primarily patients with a relatively low
29|tumor burden.9,10 Definitions of a high burden of
30|disease have included the presence of visceral
31|metastases, a bone-metastasis burden categorized
32|by site (beyond the axial skeleton) or by a high
33|number of lesions, or a combination of these.9,11,12
34|In this study, the E3805 study, patients received
35|ADT alone or ADT plus docetaxel at the begin-
36|ning of ADT for metastatic hormone-sensitive
37|prostate cancer, and stratification was performed
38|prospectively according to high or low burden of
39|metastatic disease.
40|Methods
41|Study Oversight
42|The primary objective of the E3805 study was to
43|determine whether docetaxel therapy at the be-
44|ginning of ADT for metastatic hormone-sensitive
45|prostate cancer would result in longer overall
46|survival than that with ADT alone. The study was
47|designed in 2005 by the Eastern Cooperative On-
48|cology Group (ECOG; now part of ECOG-ACRIN)
49|and was approved by the institutional review
50|board at each participating institution. The study
51|was coordinated by the ECOG-ACRIN Cancer
52|Research Group. The ECOG-ACRIN Statistical
53|Center collected the data and was the leading
54|cooperative group and data coordinating center.
55|The first two authors attest that the study was
56|conducted and monitored as specified by the
57|protocol. The first author wrote the first draft of
58|the manuscript, with subsequent contributions
59|by all the coauthors. The authors vouch for the
60|accuracy and completeness of the data presented.
61|The protocol with the statistical analysis plan
62|is available with the full text of this article at
63|NEJM.org. Sanofi donated the docetaxel for
64|early use (i.e., before progression during ADT)
65|and provided a grant to ECOG-ACRIN but had
66|no role in the design of the protocol, the collec-
67|tion or analysis of the data, or the preparation of
68|the manuscript.
69|Patients
70|Patients were enrolled by ECOG-ACRIN, the
71|Southwest Oncology Group, the Alliance for
72|Clinical Trials in Oncology, and NRG Oncology
73|(a merged group that includes the National Sur-
74|gical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project, the Ra-
75|diation Therapy Oncology Group, and the Gyne-
76|cologic Oncology Group) and through the Clinical
77|Trials Support Unit. Eligible patients had a
78|pathological diagnosis of prostate cancer or a
79|clinical scenario consistent with prostate cancer
80|with an elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
81|level; radiologic evidence of metastatic disease;
82|and an ECOG performance-status score of 0, 1,
83|or 2 (on a scale from 0 to 5, with higher scores
84|indicating greater disability; patients with a score
85|of 2 were eligible if the decrement in function-
86|ing was due to prostate cancer). Prior adjuvant
87|ADT was allowed if the duration of therapy was
88|24 months or less and progression had occurred
89|more than 12 months after completion of ther-
90|apy. Patients who were receiving ADT for meta-
91|static disease were eligible if there was no evidence
92|of progression and treatment had commenced
93|within 120 days before randomization. Organ
94|function that was adequate for docetaxel treat-
95|ment was required (details are provided in the
96|protocol). All patients provided written informed
97|consent in accordance with institutional and
98|federal guidelines.
99|Treatment Plan, Stratification,
100|and Randomization
101|Patients were randomly assigned to ADT alone
102|or to combination therapy with ADT plus doce
103|taxel at a dose of 75 mg per square meter of
104|body-surface area given every 3 weeks for six

4|cycles, with premedication with 8 mg of oral
5|dexamethasone at 12 hours, 3 hours, and 1 hour
6|before docetaxel infusion. Daily prednisone was
7|not required. Patients were stratified according
8|to age (<70 years vs. ≥70 years), ECOG perfor-
9|mance-status score (0 or 1 vs. 2), and planned
10|use of combined androgen blockade for more
11|than 30 days (yes vs. no) or agents approved for
12|prevention of skeletal-related events in castration-
13|resistant disease (zoledronic acid or denosumab)
14|(yes vs. no). Patients were also stratified accord-
15|ing to the duration of prior adjuvant ADT (<12
16|months vs. ≥12 months) and the extent of metas-
17|tases (high volume [defined as the presence of
18|visceral metastases or ≥4 bone lesions with ≥1
19|beyond the vertebral bodies and pelvis] vs. low
20|volume). Patients were required to take at least
21|500 mg of oral calcium carbonate and at least
22|400 IU of vitamin D per day.
23|Dose Modifications
24|No dose modifications of ADT were allowed,
25|and the use of a nonsteroidal antiandrogen with
26|castration (medical or surgical) at the time of
27|initiation of therapy was at the discretion of the
28|investigator. Intermittent hormonal therapy was
29|not allowed. For docetaxel, no more than two
30|dose modifications (decreases to 65 mg per
31|square meter and 55 mg per square meter) were
32|allowed. Dose adjustments were made according
33|to the organ system that showed the greatest de-
34|gree of toxic effects, which were graded accord-
35|ing to the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Com-
36|mon Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events
37|(CTCAE; version 3.0 until September 2011 and
38|version 4.0 thereafter). Details on dosing are
39|provided in the protocol. If a dose was reduced
40|owing to toxic effects, it was not increased sub-
41|sequently, and docetaxel was discontinued if
42|administration was delayed longer than 3 weeks
43|from the scheduled day of dosing. The use of
44|growth factors was at the discretion of the inves-
45|tigator.
46|Monitoring of Toxic Effects and Efficacy
47|Patients assigned to combination therapy were
48|seen every 3 weeks during the period of docetaxel
49|administration and then every 3 months. Patients
50|assigned to ADT alone were seen every 3 months.
51|For the reporting of serious adverse events to the
52|NCI and to guide dose modifications, CTCAE
53|version 3.0 was used until September 2011, at
54|which time the study began using version 4.0. To
55|ensure consistency, case-report forms for toxic
56|effects that were recorded in the study database
57|retained the use of version 3.0. All grade 3 or
58|higher toxic effects in the combination group
59|were captured, and an attribution of relatedness
60|to study therapy was made by the local investiga-
61|tors. Adverse events among patients assigned to
62|ADT alone were not routinely documented, al-
63|though major adverse events were to be reported.
64|PSA levels were measured at each scheduled
65|visit. Imaging (computed tomography [CT] of
66|the abdomen and pelvis, technetium-99m bone
67|scanning, and radiography or CT of the chest)
68|was performed at baseline and at the time of
69|documented castration resistance or as clinically
70|indicated. Disease progression on imaging was
71|determined according to the Response Evaluation
72|Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.013
73|(the criteria are summarized in the protocol). A
74|complete serologic response was defined as a
75|PSA level of less than 0.2 ng per milliliter on two
76|consecutive measurements at least 4 weeks apart.
77|Serologic progression was defined as an increase
78|in the PSA level of more than 50% above the
79|nadir reached after the initiation of ADT, with
80|two consecutive increases at least 2 weeks apart.
81|The date of a first recorded increase of more
82|than 50% above the nadir was deemed the date
83|of progression. If the nadir level was less than
84|2 ng per milliliter, a minimum increase of more
85|than 2 ng per milliliter was required.
86|All time-to-event end points were determined
87|from the time of randomization. Overall survival
88|was defined as the time until death from any
89|cause. The time to castration-resistant prostate
90|cancer was defined as the time until document-
91|ed clinical or serologic progression with a testos-
92|terone level of less than 50 ng per deciliter (or
93|source documentation of medical castration or
94|surgical castration). The time to clinical pro-
95|gression was defined as the time until increas-
96|ing symptoms of bone metastases; progression
97|according to RECIST, version 1.0; or clinical
98|deterioration due to cancer according to the in-
99|vestigator's opinion.
100|Statistical Analysis
101|The study underwent two major amendments
102|(details are provided in the protocol); in all ver-
103|sions, an intention-to-treat analysis plan was
104|used. With each amendment, the sample size

5|power to detect a 33.3% difference in median
6|overall survival between the combination group
7|and the ADT-alone group, with the use of a
8|stratified log-rank test at a one-sided alpha level
9|of 2.5%. At study inception, only patients with
10|high-volume disease were to be enrolled, and the
11|sample size was to be 568 patients. After com-
12|pletion of enrollment in the NCI-sponsored
13|S9346 trial,4 an amendment to the E3805 study
14|was made in July 2008, after 53 patients had been
15|enrolled, to include patients with low-volume
16|disease. A prospective stratification of high vol-
17|ume versus low volume of metastatic disease
18|was added, and the sample size was increased to
19|600 patients. The final amendment was made in
20|December 2011, after 579 patients had been en-
21|rolled, to reflect new data documenting an in-
22|crease in median overall survival owing to the
23|use of PSA in the detection and monitoring of
24|disease activity5 (initial projections were based
25|on studies from the pre-PSA era) and to address
26|the September 2011 report of the data and safety
27|monitoring committee, which noted that 70% of
28|enrolled patients had high-volume disease. The
29|final design required the enrollment of 780 pa-
30|tients, with projections of median overall sur-
31|vival with ADT alone of 33 months among pa-
32|tients with high-volume disease and 67 months
33|among patients with low-volume disease.
34|Interim analyses were to be performed before
35|all semiannual meetings of the data and safety
36|monitoring committee starting when approxi-
37|mately 25% of the planned full information was
38|obtained and continuing until either the criteria
39|for early stopping were met or full information
40|was obtained (after 399 deaths). The study was
41|monitored for early stopping for futility with the
42|use of repeated-confidence-interval methods.14 At
43|each interim analysis, the nominal (1 - [2 × alpha])
44|confidence interval for the hazard ratio for death
45|in the comparison of the combination-therapy
46|group with the ADT-alone group was computed.
47|For a given analysis time (information fraction),
48|alpha was set at the nominal one-sided signifi-
49|cance level of the use function boundary. Infor-
50|mation from interim analyses was reviewed by
51|members of the independent data and safety
52|monitoring committee, who determined wheth-
53|er efficacy or futility had been demonstrated and
54|who decided whether the study should be stopped
55|and the results reported early.
56|Descriptive statistics were used to characterize
57|patients at study entry. Kaplan-Meier estimates15
58|were used for event-time distributions. Cox pro-
59|portional-hazard models,16 stratified according
60|to the factors described above, were used to esti-
61|mate hazard ratios for time-to-event end points.
62|Stratified log-rank tests17 were used to compare
63|event-time distributions between the two groups.
64|Response rates were compared with the use of
65|Fisher's exact test.18 An intention-to-treat analy-
66|sis was conducted that included all randomly
67|assigned patients regardless of eligibility and
68|treatment status. P values are two-sided, and con-
69|fidence intervals are at the 95% level.
70|Results
71|Patients
72|From July 2006 through December 2012, a total
73|of 790 patients were enrolled and underwent ran-
74|domization. Ten patients were ineligible, 7 had
75|incomplete information to assess eligibility, and
76|6 patients in the combination group did not
77|start the assigned therapy (Fig. S1 in the Supple-
78|mentary Appendix, available at NEJM.org). All
79|randomly assigned patients were followed and
80|included in the primary analysis of their assigned
81|group. At the planned interim analysis in Octo-
82|ber 2013, a total of 53% of the planned full in-
83|formation had been obtained, prespecified crite-
84|ria for significance had been met, and the data
85|were released by the data and safety monitoring
86|committee. This report represents data with a
87|cutoff date for survival of December 23, 2013;
88|the median follow-up was 28.9 months, with
89|136 deaths in the ADT-alone group and 101
90|deaths in the combination group. All other data
91|reflect the database as of December 23, 2014.
92|Patient characteristics were well balanced be-

102|scores indicating a more aggressive form of pros-
103|tate cancer and a worse prognosis). In both

1|n engl j med 373;8 nejm.org August 20, 2015
2|745
3|Chemohormonal Therapy in Prostate Cancer
4|docetaxel given at the time ADT was initiated for
5|hormone-sensitive disease resulted in better can-
6|cer control than that with ADT alone, with a
7|longer time to the development of castration resis-
8|tance, a higher rate of decrease of the PSA level
9|to less than 0.2 ng per milliliter at 12 months, a
10|lower number of prostate-cancer deaths, and
11|substantially longer overall survival. The longer
12|overall survival than that with ADT alone was
13|achieved despite the fact that almost half the 287
14|patients who received ADT alone and then met
15|the criteria for castration resistance received
16|docetaxel at the time of disease progression
17|along with other therapies that prolong overall
18|survival in patients with metastatic castration-
19|resistant prostate cancer.
20|The definition of high-volume disease used
21|for this protocol was a combination of features
22|from prior classifications. All the definitions
23|included the presence of nonnodal, soft-tissue
24|visceral disease as a predictor of poor prognosis.
25|This protocol made use of sites of bone metas-
26|tases and the number of metastases to avoid
27|classifying patients with three or fewer sites as
28|having high-volume disease even if one lesion
29|was beyond the vertebrae and pelvis (any lesion
30|beyond the vertebrae and pelvis, irrespective of
31|total lesion count, would be classified as "exten-
32|sive" according to the definition of the South-
33|west Oncology Group4). In the subgroup of pa-
34|tients with high-volume disease, the median
35|overall survival was 17.0 months longer in the
36|combination group than in the ADT-alone group
37|(49.2 months vs. 32.2 months). On the basis of
38|an unpublished analysis of data from the S9346
39|trial5 we had projected a median survival of
40|33 months among patients with high-volume
41|disease (according to the definition used in our
42|protocol) in the ADT-alone group, and as such,
43|the definition was reproducible across two phase
44|3 studies conducted in a similar time period.
45|A previously reported randomized study in-
46|volving 380 patients (the GETUG-AFU 15 study),
47|which had a similar design to that of the current
48|study, did not detect longer overall survival with
49|combination therapy.10 The median overall sur-
50|vival was longer than in our study - 54.2 months
51|with ADT alone (which suggests that the study
52|had a different case mix than that in our study)
53|- and was first analyzed in 2011, before there
54|was widespread access to newer therapies that
55|have been shown to prolong overall survival
56|among patients with castration-resistant pros-
57|tate cancer. In the GETUG-AFU 15 study, the
58|time to progression was longer, the number of
59|prostate-cancer deaths was smaller, and the num-
60|ber of treatment-related deaths was larger (4 of
61|195 patients) with early docetaxel therapy than
62|with ADT alone. The Medical Research Council
63|STAMPEDE trial will add further data on the
64|role of docetaxel in hormone-sensitive prostate
65|cancer; to date, the overall survival in the ADT-
66|alone group in that study is 42 months,26 a find-
67|ing similar to that in our study.
68|In conclusion, the combination of standard
69|ADT and six cycles of docetaxel resulted in sig-
70|nificantly longer overall survival than that with
71|standard ADT alone in men with hormone-sensi-
72|tive metastatic prostate cancer. The clinical
73|benefit at this early analysis was more pro-
74|nounced among patients with a higher burden of
75|disease.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

was adjusted so that the study would have 80%
power to detect a 33.3% difference in median
overall survival between the combination group
and the ADT-alone group, with the use of a
stratified log-rank test at a one-sided alpha level
of 2.5%. At study inception, only patients with
high-volume disease were to be enrolled, and the
sample size was to be 568 patients. After com-
pletion of enrollment in the NCI-sponsored
S9346 trial,4 an amendment to the E3805 study
was made in July 2008, after 53 patients had been
enrolled, to include patients with low-volume
disease. A prospective stratification of high vol-
ume versus low volume of metastatic disease
was added, and the sample size was increased to
600 patients. The final amendment was made in
December 2011, after 579 patients had been en-
rolled, to reflect new data documenting an in-
crease in median overall survival owing to the
use of PSA in the detection and monitoring of
disease activity5 (initial projections were based
on studies from the pre-PSA era) and to address
the September 2011 report of the data and safety
monitoring committee, which noted that 70% of
enrolled patients had high-volume disease. The
final design required the enrollment of 780 pa-
tients, with projections of median overall sur-
vival with ADT alone of 33 months among pa-
tients with high-volume disease and 67 months
among patients with low-volume disease.
Interim analyses were to be performed before
all semiannual meetings of the data and safety
monitoring committee starting when approxi-
mately 25% of the planned full information was
obtained and continuing until either the criteria
for early stopping were met or full information
was obtained (after 399 deaths). The study was
monitored for early stopping for futility with the
use of repeated-confidence-interval methods.14 At
each interim analysis, the nominal (1 - [2 × alpha])
confidence interval for the hazard ratio for death
in the comparison of the combination-therapy
group with the ADT-alone group was computed.
For a given analysis time (information fraction),
alpha was set at the nominal one-sided signifi-
cance level of the use function boundary. Infor-
mation from interim analyses was reviewed by
members of the independent data and safety
monitoring committee, who determined wheth-
er efficacy or futility had been demonstrated and
who decided whether the study should be stopped
and the results reported early.
Descriptive statistics were used to characterize
patients at study entry. Kaplan-Meier estimates15
were used for event-time distributions. Cox pro-
portional-hazard models,16 stratified according
to the factors described above, were used to esti-
mate hazard ratios for time-to-event end points.
Stratified log-rank tests17 were used to compare
event-time distributions between the two groups.
Response rates were compared with the use of
Fisher's exact test.18 An intention-to-treat analy-
sis was conducted that included all randomly
assigned patients regardless of eligibility and
treatment status. P values are two-sided, and con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level.

Patients
From July 2006 through December 2012, a total
of 790 patients were enrolled and underwent ran-
domization. Ten patients were ineligible, 7 had
incomplete information to assess eligibility, and
6 patients in the combination group did not
start the assigned therapy (Fig. S1 in the Supple-
mentary Appendix, available at NEJM.org). All
randomly assigned patients were followed and
included in the primary analysis of their assigned
group. At the planned interim analysis in Octo-
ber 2013, a total of 53% of the planned full in-

The protocol does not explicitly state that investigators could not access forthcoming assignments, so probable yes is more appropriate than a definitive yes.
unknowns: The protocol does not explicitly describe access controls over the sequence before a participant's registration was complete.

If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.

sections.excerpt: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.2
sections.excerpt: If carers or people delivering the interventions are aware of the assigned intervention then its implementation, or administration of non-protocol interventions, may differ between the intervention groups. Blinding may prevent such differences. If randomized allocation was not concealed, then it is likely that carers and people delivering the interventions were aware of participants’ assigned intervention during the trial.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.3
sections.excerpt: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Answer ‘No’ or ‘Probably no’ if there were changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol, such as non-adherence to intervention, but these are consistent with what could occur outside the trial context. The answer ‘No information’ may be appropriate.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.4
sections.excerpt: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context will impact on the intervention effect estimate if they affect the outcome, but not otherwise.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.5
sections.excerpt: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context are more likely to impact on intervention effect estimate if they are not balanced between the intervention groups.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.6
sections.excerpt: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.7
sections.excerpt: This question addresses whether the number of participants who were analysed in the wrong intervention group, or excluded from the analysis, was sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact on the result. It is not possible to specify a precise rule: there may be potential for substantial impact even if fewer than 5% of participants were analysed in the wrong group or excluded, if the outcome is rare or if exclusions are strongly related to prognostic factors.

questions.bias_construct: Whether carers and people delivering interventions were aware of participants' assigned intervention.
considerations: Assess the people delivering interventions, not merely outcome assessors.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when carers or intervention personnel knew assignment, including when participant side effects or toxicities revealed it. If randomized allocation was not concealed, awareness by carers and delivery personnel is likely.
evidence_needed: A direct report of blinding or awareness by carers and people delivering the intervention, plus the allocation process when it bears on their awareness.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when awareness of carers or delivery personnel cannot be determined.

questions.bias_construct: Whether deviations inconsistent with protocol arose because of the trial context.
considerations: Side-effect-related compromised blinding counts only when resulting changes were protocol-inconsistent and context-caused.

Subsequent treatment, rescue treatment, or cross-over is not itself a deviation for the effect of assignment: establish both protocol inconsistency and a trial-context cause before answering affirmatively.

Neutral contrast: protocol-permitted rescue after progression is ordinary subsequent care; prohibited rescue encouraged by trial staff is a candidate trial-context deviation. Change only the protocol-consistency and cause premises before changing the reasoning.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes only after establishing both that the change was inconsistent with the protocol and that the trial context caused it; identify both premises in the justification. Answer no or probably no when no such deviation occurred, including ordinary non-adherence outside the trial context, protocol-consistent changes, and protocol-permitted subsequent care after progression.
evidence_needed: Evidence linking the deviation to recruitment, engagement, or trial personnel and showing it was inconsistent with the protocol.

questions.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.

A post-randomization exclusion of an eligible participant remains an analysis concern whether it happened before the endpoint was measured or after an outcome value was recorded. Record that timing separately: an outcome not collected may also matter to D3, while an observed value omitted from the assignment analysis is not thereby missing outcome data. Judge 2.7 from the excluded participants, reasons, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance for this Result.
questions.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. Consider naive per-protocol, as-treated, and post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate; post-randomization exclusion of ineligible participants may be appropriate when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment.
evidence_needed: The actual analysis population and grouping rule: who was assigned, who was analysed in each group, who was excluded or reassigned after randomization, and why.
invalid_shortcuts: an ITT label without its population
a per-protocol label without the analysis population
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an incomplete analysis description alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment about appropriateness.
questions.official_guidance: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.

was adjusted so that the study would have 80%
power to detect a 33.3% difference in median
overall survival between the combination group
and the ADT-alone group, with the use of a
stratified log-rank test at a one-sided alpha level
of 2.5%. At study inception, only patients with
high-volume disease were to be enrolled, and the
sample size was to be 568 patients. After com-
pletion of enrollment in the NCI-sponsored
S9346 trial,4 an amendment to the E3805 study
was made in July 2008, after 53 patients had been
enrolled, to include patients with low-volume
disease. A prospective stratification of high vol-
ume versus low volume of metastatic disease
was added, and the sample size was increased to
600 patients. The final amendment was made in
December 2011, after 579 patients had been en-
rolled, to reflect new data documenting an in-
crease in median overall survival owing to the
use of PSA in the detection and monitoring of
disease activity5 (initial projections were based
on studies from the pre-PSA era) and to address
the September 2011 report of the data and safety
monitoring committee, which noted that 70% of
enrolled patients had high-volume disease. The
final design required the enrollment of 780 pa-
tients, with projections of median overall sur-
vival with ADT alone of 33 months among pa-
tients with high-volume disease and 67 months
among patients with low-volume disease.
Interim analyses were to be performed before
all semiannual meetings of the data and safety
monitoring committee starting when approxi-
mately 25% of the planned full information was
obtained and continuing until either the criteria
for early stopping were met or full information
was obtained (after 399 deaths). The study was
monitored for early stopping for futility with the
use of repeated-confidence-interval methods.14 At
each interim analysis, the nominal (1 - [2 × alpha])
confidence interval for the hazard ratio for death
in the comparison of the combination-therapy
group with the ADT-alone group was computed.
For a given analysis time (information fraction),
alpha was set at the nominal one-sided signifi-
cance level of the use function boundary. Infor-
mation from interim analyses was reviewed by
members of the independent data and safety
monitoring committee, who determined wheth-
er efficacy or futility had been demonstrated and
who decided whether the study should be stopped
and the results reported early.
Descriptive statistics were used to characterize
patients at study entry. Kaplan-Meier estimates15
were used for event-time distributions. Cox pro-
portional-hazard models,16 stratified according
to the factors described above, were used to esti-
mate hazard ratios for time-to-event end points.
Stratified log-rank tests17 were used to compare
event-time distributions between the two groups.
Response rates were compared with the use of
Fisher's exact test.18 An intention-to-treat analy-
sis was conducted that included all randomly
assigned patients regardless of eligibility and
treatment status. P values are two-sided, and con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level.
Results
Patients
From July 2006 through December 2012, a total
of 790 patients were enrolled and underwent ran-
domization. Ten patients were ineligible, 7 had
incomplete information to assess eligibility, and
6 patients in the combination group did not
start the assigned therapy (Fig. S1 in the Supple-
mentary Appendix, available at NEJM.org). All
randomly assigned patients were followed and
included in the primary analysis of their assigned
group. At the planned interim analysis in Octo-
ber 2013, a total of 53% of the planned full in-
formation had been obtained, prespecified crite-
ria for significance had been met, and the data
were released by the data and safety monitoring
committee. This report represents data with a
cutoff date for survival of December 23, 2013;
the median follow-up was 28.9 months, with
136 deaths in the ADT-alone group and 101
deaths in the combination group. All other data
reflect the database as of December 23, 2014.
Patient characteristics were well balanced be-
tween the two groups (Table 1). The median age
was 64 years (range, 36 to 88) in the combina-
tion group and 63 years (range, 39 to 91) in the
ADT-alone group. In both groups, approximately
85% of the patients were white, approximately
70% had an ECOG performance-status score of 0,
approximately 65% had high-volume disease, and
approximately 60% had a Gleason score of 8 or
higher (on a scale from 2 to 10, with higher
scores indicating a more aggressive form of pros-

The report describes distinct assigned treatments: ADT alone versus ADT plus docetaxel, including repeated docetaxel administration and dose changes. answers.justification: The supplement's flow diagram reports five patient withdrawals/refusals before protocol therapy in the docetaxel group and one medical decision; these occurred after allocation and are consistent with some participants not implementing their assigned regimen in the trial context. The exact count is not fully clear because the main report says six did not start while the flow diagram lists an additional case with no treatment information. This supports only a probable judgment that trial context contributed; individual reasons are not given.
unknowns: Reasons for patient refusal or medical decisions are not reported, so the link to trial context is uncertain.

answers.justification: Not receiving early docetaxel in the assigned combination group could plausibly affect overall survival, the approved time-to-death outcome. The small number and uncertainty about reasons limit confidence in the size of any effect.

evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

was adjusted so that the study would have 80%
power to detect a 33.3% difference in median
overall survival between the combination group
and the ADT-alone group, with the use of a
stratified log-rank test at a one-sided alpha level
of 2.5%. At study inception, only patients with
high-volume disease were to be enrolled, and the
sample size was to be 568 patients. After com-
pletion of enrollment in the NCI-sponsored
S9346 trial,4 an amendment to the E3805 study
was made in July 2008, after 53 patients had been
enrolled, to include patients with low-volume
disease. A prospective stratification of high vol-
ume versus low volume of metastatic disease
was added, and the sample size was increased to
600 patients. The final amendment was made in
December 2011, after 579 patients had been en-
rolled, to reflect new data documenting an in-
crease in median overall survival owing to the
use of PSA in the detection and monitoring of
disease activity5 (initial projections were based
on studies from the pre-PSA era) and to address
the September 2011 report of the data and safety
monitoring committee, which noted that 70% of
enrolled patients had high-volume disease. The
final design required the enrollment of 780 pa-
tients, with projections of median overall sur-
vival with ADT alone of 33 months among pa-
tients with high-volume disease and 67 months
among patients with low-volume disease.
Interim analyses were to be performed before
all semiannual meetings of the data and safety
monitoring committee starting when approxi-
mately 25% of the planned full information was
obtained and continuing until either the criteria
for early stopping were met or full information
was obtained (after 399 deaths). The study was
monitored for early stopping for futility with the
use of repeated-confidence-interval methods.14 At
each interim analysis, the nominal (1 - [2 × alpha])
confidence interval for the hazard ratio for death
in the comparison of the combination-therapy
group with the ADT-alone group was computed.
For a given analysis time (information fraction),
alpha was set at the nominal one-sided signifi-
cance level of the use function boundary. Infor-
mation from interim analyses was reviewed by
members of the independent data and safety
monitoring committee, who determined wheth-
er efficacy or futility had been demonstrated and
who decided whether the study should be stopped
and the results reported early.
Descriptive statistics were used to characterize
patients at study entry. Kaplan-Meier estimates15
were used for event-time distributions. Cox pro-
portional-hazard models,16 stratified according
to the factors described above, were used to esti-
mate hazard ratios for time-to-event end points.
Stratified log-rank tests17 were used to compare
event-time distributions between the two groups.
Response rates were compared with the use of
Fisher's exact test.18 An intention-to-treat analy-
sis was conducted that included all randomly
assigned patients regardless of eligibility and
treatment status. P values are two-sided, and con-

From July 2006 through December 2012, a total

answers.justification: For the approved survival cutoff, the article states that all 790 randomized patients were followed and included in the assigned-group primary analysis, and reports 136 and 101 deaths by arm. The registry defines survival follow-up through death or date last known alive. The later supplement flow diagram (as of December 23, 2014) records 3 documented losses to follow-up and 25 withdrawals/refusals across arms, but it does not establish that these participants lacked vital-status data by the earlier December 23, 2013 survival cutoff. The evidence supports that data were probably available for nearly all randomized participants, while exact arm-specific vital-status availability at the cutoff is not reported.
unknowns: The number with unknown vital status at the December 23, 2013 survival cutoff is not explicitly reported.
Later follow-up documentation reports loss to follow-up and withdrawals, but does not clarify whether vital status at the earlier approved cutoff was unavailable for these participants.

counterevidence.implication: The later flow diagram records some loss to follow-up and withdrawal/refusal, so complete ongoing follow-up cannot be assumed; it does not specify whether mortality data were unavailable at the earlier outcome cutoff.

questions.wording: Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when appropriateness of the measurement method cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The measurement method is unsuitable, insensitive, or poorly valid for this outcome.
The measurement method is appropriate for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

Measurement susceptibility concerns whether the method can validly and sensitively measure this outcome. It is distinct from assessor awareness, detection opportunity, and whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.

A standardized instrument can still involve judgment in elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment. Preserve component-specific Evidence and uncertainty for mixed objective and subjective components.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

Differences between intervention groups may arise because of ‘diagnostic detection bias’ in the context of passive collection of outcome data, or if an intervention involves additional visits to a healthcare provider.

sections.excerpt: Knowledge of the assigned intervention could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement, and intervention provider decision outcomes. They are unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes that do not involve judgement, for example all-cause mortality.

sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which knowledge of intervention status could have influenced outcome assessment but there is no reason to believe that it did from those in which knowledge of intervention status was likely to influence outcome assessment. When there are strong levels of belief in either beneficial or harmful effects of the intervention, it is more likely that the outcome was influenced.

answer_anchors.text: Measurement or ascertainment could differ between intervention groups.
The same comparable measurement or ascertainment was used between groups.

questions.bias_construct: Whether measurement or ascertainment of the outcome could have differed between intervention groups.
considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.

Tie every monitoring difference to the approved event. Extra visits for toxicity monitoring do not establish differential measurement of mortality when death is captured through the same complete registry in both groups; those same visits may change detection of a lab-detected toxicity measured at those visits. State any mortality-specific pathway if one is supported.

For adverse events, compare the actual start and end of the AE observation window, visit schedule, post-treatment follow-up, and ascertainment method with the approved safety window. Treatment duration, median progression-free survival, or a treatment-emergent label alone does not establish when or how adverse events were observed.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.
evidence_needed: Methods, thresholds, timing, and opportunities for outcome ascertainment in each intervention group, plus the pathway connecting any opportunity difference to differential detection.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when comparability of measurement or ascertainment cannot be assessed.
questions.official_guidance: Comparable methods of outcome measurement involve the same measurement methods and thresholds, used at comparable time points. Differences between intervention groups may arise because of ‘diagnostic detection bias’ in the context of passive collection of outcome data, or if an intervention involves additional visits to a healthcare provider.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.
Outcome assessors knew the intervention received.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome assessors were aware of the intervention received, when 4.1 and 4.2 are not yes/probably yes. Identify the assessor's identity and role: who determines the approved outcome at the relevant time point, not merely who records it.
considerations: The assessor can be a participant, intervention provider, or independent observer.

This asks only whether the relevant assessor knew assignment. It does not establish that the measurement was susceptible to bias, that detection opportunities differed, or that knowledge likely changed the assessment; those are separate questions.
Unknown assessor identity or awareness does not prevent conditional reasoning about whether the measurement could be influenced if awareness existed.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when the outcome assessor was blinded to intervention status. For participant-reported outcomes, the participant is the outcome assessor, so participant blinding can determine this answer. This question is applicable only after the stated activation conditions.
evidence_needed: Who assessed the outcome and whether that assessor was blinded to intervention status.
invalid_shortcuts: participant blinding without identifying the outcome assessor
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when assessor awareness cannot be determined; do not infer blinding from an objective endpoint or from blinding elsewhere in the trial.

answer_anchors.text: Knowledge of intervention could influence assessment.
The outcome assessment could not be influenced by knowledge of intervention.

questions.bias_construct: Whether assessment could have been influenced by knowledge of intervention received. Keep assessor awareness separate from the mechanism by which awareness could change a judgement.
considerations: Assess whether knowledge could influence this outcome. Evidence that influence actually occurred belongs to 4.5; its absence does not resolve 4.4.

Possible influence requires a judgement or reporting pathway through which assessor awareness could matter. Awareness alone is not a measurement difference, and a susceptible outcome does not by itself show that influence was possible in this assessment.
When a composite mixes objective and subjective components, assess each component's pathway separately and retain uncertainty where a component-specific link is unresolved.
questions.decision_rule: Knowledge could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving judgement, and intervention-provider decisions; it is unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes without judgement, such as all-cause mortality. A standardized instrument does not remove judgment from elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment.
evidence_needed: Outcome type, assessor role, degree of judgement, and whether knowledge of assignment could change assessment.
invalid_shortcuts: participant blinding without identifying the outcome assessor
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when possible influence cannot be determined; this question is conditional on awareness in 4.3.
questions.official_guidance: Knowledge of the assigned intervention could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement, and intervention provider decision outcomes. They are unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes that do not involve judgement, for example all-cause mortality.

questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 4.3: Could assessment of the outcome have been influenced by knowledge of intervention received?

answer_anchors.text: Knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.
Knowledge could have influenced assessment but it was not likely to do so.

questions.bias_construct: Whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced outcome assessment. Require evidence or strong beliefs plus a judgement opportunity; awareness alone does not establish influence.
considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.
Objective components can provide valid reassurance for those components without overriding likely influence or unresolved Evidence for subjective components in the same Result.
questions.decision_rule: Distinguish possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence. Strong beliefs about benefits or harms make influence more likely, for example patient-reported symptoms or recovery assessed by an intervention provider. A standardized scale or grading rule does not by itself remove an elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment pathway.
evidence_needed: Evidence of actual influence or strong beliefs and judgement opportunities that make influence likely, given the assessor and outcome.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of influence cannot be judged; this question is conditional on possible influence in 4.4.
questions.official_guidance: This question distinguishes between situations in which knowledge of intervention status could have influenced outcome assessment but there is no reason to believe that it did from those in which knowledge of intervention status was likely to influence outcome assessment. When there are strong levels of belief in either beneficial or harmful effects of the intervention, it is more likely that the outcome was influenced.

the median time from the start of ADT to ran-
domization was 1.2 months (range, 0 to 3.9) in
the combination group and 1.3 months (range,
0 to 3.9) in the ADT-alone group.

The median overall survival was 13.6 months
longer with the addition to ADT of early docetax-
el than with ADT alone (57.6 months vs. 44.0
months; hazard ratio for death in the combina-
tion group, 0.61; 95% confidence interval [CI],
0.47 to 0.80; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A). There were 85
prostate-cancer deaths in the combination group
and 114 prostate-cancer deaths in the ADT-alone
group (Table S1 in the Supplementary Appen-
dix). The benefit at the last analysis was more
apparent in the subgroup with high-volume dis-
ease than in the overall study population
(Fig. 1B), with a median overall survival that was
17.0 months longer in the combination group
than in the ADT-alone group (49.2 months vs.
32.2 months; hazard ratio for death, 0.60; 95%
CI, 0.45 to 0.81; P<0.001). The median survival
at the time of the analysis had not been reached
in the subgroup with low-volume disease in ei-
ther study group (Fig. 1C). A benefit of docetax-
el treatment was detected in all the subgroups
analyzed (Fig. 2).

The proportion of patients who had a decrease
in the PSA level to less than 0.2 ng per milliliter
at 12 months was 27.7% in the combination
group, as compared with 16.8% in the ADT-
alone group (P<0.001) (Table 2). The median
time to the development of castration-resistant
prostate cancer (biochemical, symptomatic, or
radiographic) was 20.2 months with combina-
tion therapy, as compared with 11.7 months
with ADT alone (hazard ratio in the combina-
tion group, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.72; P<0.001)

power to detect a 33.3% difference in median
overall survival between the combination group
and the ADT-alone group, with the use of a
stratified log-rank test at a one-sided alpha level
of 2.5%. At study inception, only patients with
high-volume disease were to be enrolled, and the
sample size was to be 568 patients. After com-
pletion of enrollment in the NCI-sponsored
S9346 trial,4 an amendment to the E3805 study
was made in July 2008, after 53 patients had been
enrolled, to include patients with low-volume
disease. A prospective stratification of high vol-
ume versus low volume of metastatic disease
was added, and the sample size was increased to
600 patients. The final amendment was made in
December 2011, after 579 patients had been en-
rolled, to reflect new data documenting an in-
crease in median overall survival owing to the
use of PSA in the detection and monitoring of
disease activity5 (initial projections were based
on studies from the pre-PSA era) and to address
the September 2011 report of the data and safety
monitoring committee, which noted that 70% of
enrolled patients had high-volume disease. The
final design required the enrollment of 780 pa-
tients, with projections of median overall sur-
vival with ADT alone of 33 months among pa-
tients with high-volume disease and 67 months
among patients with low-volume disease.
Interim analyses were to be performed before
all semiannual meetings of the data and safety
monitoring committee starting when approxi-
mately 25% of the planned full information was
obtained and continuing until either the criteria
for early stopping were met or full information
was obtained (after 399 deaths). The study was
monitored for early stopping for futility with the
use of repeated-confidence-interval methods.14 At
each interim analysis, the nominal (1 - [2 × alpha])
confidence interval for the hazard ratio for death
in the comparison of the combination-therapy
group with the ADT-alone group was computed.
For a given analysis time (information fraction),
alpha was set at the nominal one-sided signifi-
cance level of the use function boundary. Infor-
mation from interim analyses was reviewed by
members of the independent data and safety
monitoring committee, who determined wheth-
er efficacy or futility had been demonstrated and
who decided whether the study should be stopped
and the results reported early.
Descriptive statistics were used to characterize
patients at study entry. Kaplan-Meier estimates15
were used for event-time distributions. Cox pro-
portional-hazard models,16 stratified according
to the factors described above, were used to esti-
mate hazard ratios for time-to-event end points.
Stratified log-rank tests17 were used to compare
event-time distributions between the two groups.
Response rates were compared with the use of
Fisher's exact test.18 An intention-to-treat analy-
sis was conducted that included all randomly
assigned patients regardless of eligibility and
treatment status. P values are two-sided, and con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level.
Results
Patients
From July 2006 through December 2012, a total
of 790 patients were enrolled and underwent ran-
domization. Ten patients were ineligible, 7 had
incomplete information to assess eligibility, and
6 patients in the combination group did not
start the assigned therapy (Fig. S1 in the Supple-
mentary Appendix, available at NEJM.org). All
randomly assigned patients were followed and
included in the primary analysis of their assigned
group. At the planned interim analysis in Octo-
ber 2013, a total of 53% of the planned full in-
formation had been obtained, prespecified crite-
ria for significance had been met, and the data
were released by the data and safety monitoring
committee. This report represents data with a
cutoff date for survival of December 23, 2013;
the median follow-up was 28.9 months, with
136 deaths in the ADT-alone group and 101
deaths in the combination group. All other data
reflect the database as of December 23, 2014.
Patient characteristics were well balanced be-
tween the two groups (Table 1). The median age
was 64 years (range, 36 to 88) in the combina-
tion group and 63 years (range, 39 to 91) in the
ADT-alone group. In both groups, approximately
85% of the patients were white, approximately
70% had an ECOG performance-status score of 0,
approximately 65% had high-volume disease, and
approximately 60% had a Gleason score of 8 or
higher (on a scale from 2 to 10, with higher
scores indicating a more aggressive form of pros-
